fragments.text: And one example of national security, the interplay of national security and the public good or the right to know is this issue of zero days. So the NSA exploits vulnerabilities in Windows, for example, that they think nobody knows about. That's where the term zero day comes from. It's that, you know, the company, in this case, Microsoft or security vendors have had zero days to respond to the vulnerability. And so the NSA was using this vulnerability as a way to spy. And then when it became public, by a hacking group out of Russia hacking a hacking group that was doing work for the NSA they published this this zero day on the internet and it enabled ransom

And, but instead they wanted the capability thinking they were the only ones smart enough to be exploiting it or not caring maybe that their enemies were exploiting it as well, but that seems unlikely. And so this is a case where the reporting, the right to know about a vulnerability in software, generally outweighs even a friendly country's surveillance or intelligence capabilities.

fragments.text: Then to just look a little bit at the obstacles or threats to our right to know, the first The first obvious one is censorship and in South Africa, we recently had some success in by the way of SLAP, which is a strategic lawsuit against public participation. And elsewhere in the world, especially in the United States, there's been legislation passed to help protect people against something like this, a frivolous lawsuit that is designed to silence, right? So you sue someone for defamation because you know that just defending the case will cost them a significant sum of money. And so, you know, you've got a justice system that is skewed towards people who have the time and the money.
